detail: p. 2206, Incidence. The infant estimate is approximately 15%. The four chromosome abnormalities listed account for the majority.
p. 2206, Incidence. The 30–40% estimate applies to most fetal series. Greater fetal loss is presented as a likely explanation for the difference from infants.
p. 2207, Genetic Testing of Fetuses With CHD. The statement gives the same lower-bound wording and 15–30% range for apparently isolated CHD on ultrasound.
p. 2207, Genetic Testing of Fetuses With CHD. The recommendation extends to all diagnosed cardiac malformations irrespective of other anomalies.
p. 2207, Genetic Testing of Fetuses With CHD. The authors discuss additional investigations, more specific recurrence estimates and decisions about termination or the intensity of postnatal care.
pp. 2206–2207, Available Genetic Testing. The limitation for balanced changes spans the page break. The next paragraph calls for disclosure of the prognostic uncertainty that testing can introduce.
p. 2206, Available Genetic Testing. The comparison concerns array CGH replacing conventional karyotyping and FISH, and describes the debate in 2014.
p. 2207, Genetic Abnormalities Associated With CHD. All four diagnoses occur in the low-aneuploidy group. The offer of testing is paired with counselling.
p. 2207, Genetic Abnormalities Associated With CHD. The text identifies VSD and AVSD as the lesions most often associated with a karyotype abnormality.
p. 2207, Genetic Abnormalities Associated With CHD. The approximately 50–70% estimate concerns trisomy 21 among fetuses with AVSD and normal situs.
p. 2207, Genetic Abnormalities Associated With CHD. The authors name both conotruncal malformations and a right arch in connection with 22q11 deletion.
p. 2207, Genetic Abnormalities Associated With CHD. The >60% estimate and recommendation for genetic evaluation apply to single or multiple cardiac tumours found in mid or late gestation.
p. 2207, Table 10, Risk column. AVSD 46–73%, TOF 7–39%, truncus 19–78%, HLHS 4–9%, TGA 0%, heterotaxy/cardiosplenic syndromes 0%. The zeros describe the tabulated series.
p. 2208, Table 11, Estimated Frequency column. The five corresponding entries are 50–90%, 35–40%, 8–35%, 25% and <1%. The last entry retains the strict inequality.

p. 2208, Extracardiac Abnormalities, Incidence. The infant ceiling is correct. The fetal figure is an upper-end observation from published reports. Presenting 50–70% as the fetal range drops that qualifier.
p. 2208, Extracardiac Abnormalities, Incidence. The source pairs VSD and tricuspid atresia with other anomalies and describes d-TGA and PA/IVS as more often isolated.

p. 2208, Incidence and Fetal Survey. A specialist detailed survey is recommended for every fetus with CHD. The preceding passage allows repeat assessment in selected cases after an initially normal extracardiac survey.

p. 2208, Fetal MRI. The question concerns extracardiac anomaly screening in a fetus with known CHD and an otherwise normal ultrasound. As written, the claim extends the uncertainty to all fetuses with normal ultrasound.

p. 2208, Rationale. The evidence gap specifically concerns recommendations for fetuses with isolated CHD. Extending that gap to all heart disease goes beyond the source. Selected use and risks from false positives are supported.
p. 2209, Cardiotocography and Nonstress Testing. Bradycardia and complete heart block are specifically identified among arrhythmias for which testing is unlikely to help.

p. 2209, Biophysical Profile. The caution about recommending widespread testing refers to the selected CHD populations just discussed, at risk of hypoxemia and acidosis. The authors consider early delivery likely with widespread testing.
p. 2209, Prenatal Counseling and Parental Stress. The four aims are supported. The team should provide support, while the inclusion of a social worker or genetic counsellor is optional.

p. 2209, Essential Elements. The recommendation is to offer counselling promptly, ideally on the same day. It specifies when the offer should be made without requiring the encounter to take place then.
p. 2209, Essential Elements. All three limitations appear in the paragraph, which specifies early gestational age as the example.
p. 2209, Essential Elements. The authors address antenatal evolution, prognosis, genetic and syndromic associations, and counselling to alleviate guilt.
pp. 2209–2210, Essential Elements. The text asks for contemporary outcome data and discussion of uncertainties, including possible advances over time.

p. 2210, Techniques. The evidence gap concerns techniques specifically for counselling after a prenatal CHD diagnosis, as understood in 2014. The unqualified statement reads as a claim about counselling in general.

p. 2210, Techniques. Checking comprehension and offering continued support are recommended. Several sessions may be needed depending on the family's circumstances. The claim turns this conditional need into a universal instruction to offer several sessions.
p. 2210, Techniques. The statement calls for discussion of termination and communication of applicable regional legal time limits. It supplies no Indian legal limit.
p. 2210, Decision Making. The two instructions are to avoid imposing the counsellor's bias and to support the family's decision.
p. 2210, Maternal and Paternal Effects. The referral and diagnostic findings concern maternal anxiety. The comparison with postnatal diagnosis describes distress in parents.

p. 2211, opening paragraph. The authors weigh maternal risk and postnatal treatment options for potentially modifiable or lethal disorders. They report no randomised controlled fetal cardiac therapy studies at the time.
